enonce_markdown: Using $Nx$: $x$ is a nurse and $Kx$: $x$ is kind, which formula best symbolises "All nurses are kind"?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A universal categorical statement "All S are P" is symbolised by a universally quantified conditional, $(x)(Sx \supset Px)$.

### Solution

"All nurses are kind" is a universal statement: for every $x$, if $x$ is a nurse then $x$ is kind.

$$(x)(Nx \supset Kx)$$

A universal statement takes a conditional, not a conjunction: $(x)(Nx \cdot Kx)$ would say that everything is a kind nurse. The existential $(\exists x)(Nx \cdot Kx)$ only says that at least one kind nurse exists, and $(x)(Kx \supset Nx)$ is the converse ("all kind things are nurses").

**Answer: c.**

enonce_markdown:
Symbolise each statement, using the given predicates.

(i) Some traders at the market are dishonest. ($Tx$: $x$ is a trader at the market; $Dx$: $x$ is dishonest)

(ii) No farmer is idle. ($Fx$: $x$ is a farmer; $Ix$: $x$ is idle)
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

"Some S are P" is $(\exists x)(Sx \cdot Px)$ and "No S are P" is $(x)(Sx \supset \sim Px)$, or equivalently $\sim(\exists x)(Sx \cdot Px)$.

### Solution

**(i)** "Some traders are dishonest" says that at least one individual is both a trader and dishonest. An existential statement uses a conjunction:

$$(\exists x)(Tx \cdot Dx)$$

**(ii)** "No farmer is idle" says that for every individual, if it is a farmer then it is not idle:

$$(x)(Fx \supset \sim Ix)$$

Equivalent form: $\sim(\exists x)(Fx \cdot Ix)$, "there is nothing that is both a farmer and idle".

enonce_markdown: Let $Mx$: $x$ is a member of the club and $Vx$: $x$ is allowed to vote. Which formula expresses "Only members are allowed to vote"?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

"Only S are P" reverses the direction of the conditional: it is symbolised $(x)(Px \supset Sx)$, "everything that is P is S".

### Solution

"Only members are allowed to vote" means that nobody outside the membership can vote, so anything allowed to vote is a member.

$$(x)(Vx \supset Mx)$$

The formula $(x)(Mx \supset Vx)$ says that all members may vote, which is the converse: it does not exclude non-members. The existential statement $(\exists x)(Mx \cdot Vx)$ only says that at least one member may vote. An existential conditional or a negated universal does not capture the restriction either.

**Answer: a.**

enonce_markdown: Let $Tx$: $x$ is a teacher and $Sx$: $x$ is strict. Which formula is equivalent to "Not every teacher is strict"?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The negation of a universal statement is an existential statement of the negated matrix: $\sim(x)\varphi x \equiv (\exists x)\sim\varphi x$, and $\sim(Tx \supset Sx) \equiv Tx \cdot \sim Sx$.

### Solution

"Not every teacher is strict" denies $(x)(Tx \supset Sx)$:

$$\sim(x)(Tx \supset Sx) \equiv (\exists x)\sim(Tx \supset Sx) \equiv (\exists x)(Tx \cdot \sim Sx)$$

so at least one teacher is not strict. The universal $(x)(Tx \supset \sim Sx)$ says that no teacher is strict, which is stronger; $(\exists x)(Tx \cdot Sx)$ says that some teacher is strict; and $(\exists x)(Tx \supset \sim Sx)$ is true as soon as one thing is not a teacher, so it does not express the idea.

**Answer: b.**

enonce_markdown: Using $Ax$: $x$ is absent from the examination and $Px$: $x$ is punished, symbolise "There is no student who is both absent and punished" in two equivalent ways, one with the existential quantifier and one with the universal quantifier, and explain in a sentence why the two forms say the same thing.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Quantifier negation: $\sim(\exists x)\varphi x \equiv (x)\sim\varphi x$. Then $\sim(Ax \cdot Px)$ is rewritten as the conditional $Ax \supset \sim Px$.

### Solution

Existential form: nothing satisfies both $Ax$ and $Px$ together.

$$\sim(\exists x)(Ax \cdot Px)$$

Universal form: for every individual, if it is absent then it is not punished.

$$(x)(Ax \supset \sim Px)$$

They are equivalent by quantifier negation: $\sim(\exists x)(Ax \cdot Px) \equiv (x)\sim(Ax \cdot Px)$, and $\sim(Ax \cdot Px) \equiv (Ax \supset \sim Px)$. Saying that no individual has both properties is the same as saying that every individual who has the first lacks the second.

enonce_markdown: Let $Px$ stand for "x is a senator" and $Dx$ for "x takes bribes". A student writes $(\exists x)(Px \supset Dx)$ for the statement "Some senators take bribes". Why is this translation faulty?

choix.texte: It says that every senator takes bribes, which is stronger than the original statement
It says that no senator takes bribes, because the conditional reverses the claim
It is false whenever there are two senators who take bribes
It is true whenever something is not a senator, so it can be true even if no senator takes bribes

corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

With the existential quantifier use the conjunction: the statement must assert that some individual has both properties. A conditional under $(\exists x)$ is made true by anything that fails the antecedent.

### Solution

The correct translation is $(\exists x)(Px \cdot Dx)$.

The student's formula is true as soon as there is **one individual that is not a senator**, because then $Px$ is false and the conditional $Px \supset Dx$ is true. It can therefore be true in a world where there is no senator who takes bribes at all, or no senators at all (the check is easy on a small domain: if nothing is a senator, $(\exists x)(Px \supset Dx)$ is true while $(\exists x)(Px \cdot Dx)$ is false). The formula does not assert that any senator exists, let alone one who takes bribes.

**Answer: d.**
